tier_reason: README Performance tables and vignettes/performance.Rmd show every claimed number (864/688/368/104 uniform and 366/355/143/125/28 normal on EPYC 7763; 2196/1918/311/213 and 739/718/235/225/43 on M1; threaded 1801, 4984, 3143), with public benchmark code (.github/workflows/benchmark.yml, tools/benchmark.R) and CPU models, but the compiler is never named (only 'an -O2 build' via R CMD INSTALL) and the numbers are first-party, so C rather than A.

corrections.caveats: None of the listed baselines (std::mt19937, xoshiro, PCG) is measured directly: competitors are R packages (dqrng, randompack, RcppZiggurat, sitmo) and base R, so numbers include R vector allocation and page faults (vignette: allocating and zeroing a 1e7 vector alone runs at about 1,250 M/s on the Linux runner; forcing 4 KiB pages cut the uniform fill from 837 to 242 M/s and the normal fill from 338 to 162). On Linux kernels in the default madvise mode zurand itself requests 2 MiB pages for outputs of 4 MiB or more while the competitors do not; the vignette's Neoverse N2 table shows zurand without that request at parity with randompack (268 vs 271 M/s uniform, 214 vs 200 normal) and 532/344 with it, so on such kernels much of the lead is page size, not generation. The EPYC runner used transparent huge pages 'always', so its rows are like-for-like on page size. Base R's runif()/rnorm() default is a Mersenne Twister with inversion, so the large gaps against it (derived from page data: about 8.3x uniform and 13x normal on EPYC, 1 thread) are largely algorithm and implementation choice. The real peer is randompack's SIMD xoshiro256++, where the single-thread lead is 1.26x (uniform, x86_64), 1.15x (M1; 0.97x for 1e5 values), and only 1.01-1.08x for normals. The threaded rows are not like-for-like (the competitors have no threaded R-level entry point, as the workflow itself says). Linux numbers come from a shared CI runner launched on demand (workflow_dispatch); the author notes GitHub's M1 runner moved by a third between runs and that zurand is tuned on Apple Silicon, and the M1 numbers were run locally. Compiler not named, so tier C rather than A despite public workflow code and stated CPU models. Brand-new repository (commits from 2026-09-27, version 0.1.0, not yet on CRAN), 0 stars; first-party numbers only.

notes: All README/vignette numbers match the record; metadata (MIT, 0 stars, 0 forks, last commit 2026-10-05, 183 commits) checked on github.com. Added shortcoming: on madvise-mode Linux kernels zurand requests 2 MiB pages for its own output and is at parity with randompack without that request (N2: 268 vs 271 M/s uniform). The 'no fused multiply-add in normal sampling' item in compiler_and_flags was not confirmed in configure or Makevars.in (no -ffp-contract flag there); left as is.

corrections.caveats: No numeric comparison on any page opened, so tier D; claims come only from search snippets (snippet only) of the authors' papers (Duff, Hogg and Lopez, NACO 2018, doi 10.3934/naco.2018014; Duff and Lopez on PaRSEC; an IJHPCA paper, doi 10.1177/1094342019888567) saying the OpenMP, StarPU and PaRSEC versions show 'comparable performance' to HSL_MA87 on a multicore architecture, i.e. parity, not a speedup. The repo has bench_kernels/ and scripts/ but no published results. Last commit 2019-08-23 (abandoned), Travis CI badge only. Fortran rather than C++; callable from C++ through its C interface (interfaces/). Low notability (6 stars). Kept as a seed record for the catalogue; a paper-access retier could add the tables.
